notes.text: If you include the meaning of the name **Mahanaim** in your translation or in a footnote, be sure it matches the way you translated **God’s camp** earlier in the verse so that it is clear why Jacob gave the place that name.

notes.text: For some languages it is more natural to use an indirect quote here, especially since Jacob is quoting the one he is talking to.
Consider whether it is more natural in your language to use a direct or indirect quote in verses 17–20a.
The idiom **cover his face** means to try to calm someone’s anger by doing something to please him. or [Perhaps Esau will stop being angry at me if I send]
If you include the meaning of the name **Israel** in your translation or in a footnote, make sure it fits with how you translate **struggled** in the following clause.
The Hebrew word for **struggled** here is more general than the word for “wrestled” in verses 24 and 25.

This rhetorical question probably means that there was no need for Jacob to ask the man what his name was; he should have known without asking. Consider whether or not it is best to use a rhetorical question here in your language.

Penuel is another name for the place that is called Peniel in verse 30. That information could be put in a footnote. Or you could use the same spelling in both verses to avoid confusion; **Penuel** is the spelling in the rest of the Old Testament.
Make sure it is clear in your translation that this is talking about eating meat from an animal, not about cannibalism.
